questions.a: 'has been living' or 'has lived' — 'since + point of time' demands perfect/perfect-continuous. A wrong answer 'is living' or 'lives' reveals the student processed the verb but not the marker — the diagnostic signature of translating from Hindi instead of reading the English signal.

questions.q: 'By the time we reached, the train ___.' Choose: left / had left / has left.
questions.a: 'had left' — 'by the time' orders two past events, so the earlier one takes past perfect. A wrong answer 'left' shows the student treats both events as simultaneous — missing the two-event ordering that 'by the time' encodes.

questions.q: Which is wrong and why: 'While I walked home, it was starting to rain.'
questions.a: The framing is inverted: 'while' wants the continuous background — 'While I was walking home, it started to rain.' A wrong answer that accepts it reveals the student knows 'while + continuous' as a slogan but cannot apply it directionally (background gets the continuous, not the interrupting event).

questions.q: Certain adverbials and structures force specific tense choices: 'since/for' demands perfect or ______, 'by the time' pairs with past perfect, 'while' frames a continuous background action.

Fill in the blank: Certain ______ and structures force specific tense choices: 'since/for' demands perfect or perfect-continuous, 'by the time' pairs with past perfect, 'while' frames a continuous background action.
Fill in the blank: Write two ______: 'I ___ here since 2019' and 'I ___ here in 2019'.
Fill in the blank: The marker is the whole game — 'since' drags the action into now (perfect), 'in ______' locks it in the past (simple past).
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can name the tense(s) licensed by since/for/by-the-time/while/already/yet/just markers, justify the choice, and spot marker–tense mismatches in editing questions.
